segments.title: Why maximal treaty demands risked alienating Japan
segments.body: Governments at Washington pursued the best immediate deal they could obtain, with too little regard for whether it would endure. A warning attributed to John Maynard Keynes about the Treaty of Versailles supplies the comparison: maximizing a settlement can create conditions for another war. In this interpretation, Versailles threatened another European conflict, while the Washington and London naval treaties helped make a future war global. Japan's imperial expansion already made confrontation likely, but a less hostile settlement could have reduced that risk and the attraction of cooperation with Germany. Japan had cleared German possessions in East Asia, served in the Mediterranean, and offered a squadron for the Grand Fleet. Its wartime contribution began earlier than America's, yet its delegates encountered restrictions resembling those imposed on a defeated power. The American battleship deployment is assessed here chiefly as a matter of national status, since the Grand Fleet had no pressing need for the additional ships.

evidence.note: Maximal bargaining may win immediate concessions while undermining a durable settlement; Japan's Allied service could have made its postwar treatment a source of grievance.

segments.summary: Japan's wartime service complicates a settlement that, in this interpretation, treated an ally as a defeated power and increased the risk of a wider war.

segments.title: Why ships and crews still require fleet training
segments.body: Capable equipment and committed personnel still need fleet-level training before they can maneuver and fight as a coherent unit. Congressional limits on training are presented as the reason American battleships reached the Grand Fleet without enough gunnery and formation experience. Equipment quality and personal commitment could not substitute for crews learning to operate together under demanding conditions. The large interwar fleet problems offer the kind of realistic, repeated exercise needed to turn material strength into readiness.

evidence.note: Restricted US training funds left battleship crews short of gunnery and maneuver practice, showing why large fleet exercises are essential to turn ships into a ready force.

segments.summary: The arrival of American battleships with limited practice supports a broader warning that cutting exercises can leave good ships and personnel operationally unready.

segments.title: The 5:5:3 ratio stopped below capital ships
segments.body: The proposed fleet ratio allocated five shares each to the Royal Navy and U.S. Navy, three to Japan, and 1.75 each to France and Italy. Japan sought a 7:10 relationship with Britain and the United States because it believed that level could prevent a quick defeat, even though their larger industrial bases would still make a prolonged war unwinnable. At a British or American capital-ship allowance of 525,000 tons, a 70 percent Japanese share would have meant 367,500 tons. American intelligence indicated that Japan would accept a lower minimum of six shares to ten, or three to five. The final 5:5:3 arrangement applied chiefly to capital ships and carriers. Below those categories, navies could build unlimited numbers of ships up to 10,000 tons, creating a strong incentive to use the whole individual-ship allowance.

evidence.note: Japan sought a 7:10 capital-ship ratio because it believed that level could prevent quick defeat, while the treaty left no aggregate tonnage limit below capital ships and carriers.

segments.summary: The treaty's famous capital-ship ratio did not impose total tonnage limits on cruisers and smaller warships, encouraging construction at the maximum permitted size.

segments.title: Washington Treaty rules for other ships
segments.body: Article 11 limited warships outside the capital-ship and carrier categories to 10,000 tons standard displacement. It exempted vessels employed on fleet duties or as transports and auxiliaries if they had not been built as fighting ships or taken under government control for fighting purposes in peacetime. Article 12 set an eight-inch gun ceiling for newly laid-down warships other than capital ships. Article 13 barred reconverting ships designated for scrapping into warships, subject to its stated Article 9 exception. Article 14 allowed merchant decks to be stiffened for guns up to six inches but otherwise prohibited peacetime preparations for warship conversion. Article 16 required disclosure of construction contracts for non-signatory powers, including contract and keel-laying dates and specified ship details. Article 17 prohibited a belligerent signatory from using warships built for another power that remained undelivered within its jurisdiction. Article 18 separately prohibited disposal by gift, sale, or other transfer that would place a warship in a foreign navy, without limiting that prohibition to wartime.

evidence.note: Articles 11 through 18 limited non-capital warship size and guns, regulated auxiliaries and merchant conversion, and restricted foreign construction, wartime use, and transfer.

segments.summary: The treaty combined limits on warship size and armament with exceptions for auxiliaries, restricted merchant conversions, and rules for foreign construction and transfers.

segments.title: British ship exports and a possible County-class building programme
segments.body: Britain supported its large naval-industrial base partly by building warships for foreign customers. Those customers did not necessarily want the details of their ships disclosed to rival powers, so the treaty's reporting requirements could weaken that business. Merchant-conversion restrictions also affected a Royal Navy that relied on armed merchant cruisers to supplement its cruiser fleet. One proposed British response is to use the absence of an aggregate cruiser limit to build at least four County-class ships a year, possibly six, as large and powerful as the individual limits allowed. This counterfactual programme could have kept work flowing through the yards, although cruiser construction would not have supported armour production as fully as battleship orders.

evidence.note: Disclosure rules threatened Britain's foreign warship business, and merchant-conversion limits constrained a traditional cruiser supplement; a proposed programme of four to six County-class cruisers a year would keep yards busy but support less armour production than battleships.

segments.summary: Disclosing ships built for foreign customers could discourage orders, while unrestricted cruiser numbers offered a way to keep British yards working.

segments.title: Could six-inch gun supports prepare merchant ships for torpedoes?
segments.body: Article 14 permitted merchant decks to be stiffened for guns no larger than six inches. One proposed way to exploit that allowance is to design a twin six-inch mounting whose weight matches or exceeds that of a triple torpedo launcher. Deck support prepared for the permitted gun installation could then accommodate the torpedo outfit envisaged for wartime. The proposal responds to the lack of torpedoes on British armed merchant cruisers and the stronger opponents they could encounter in the Second World War. It is a counterfactual design suggestion, and the discussion does not establish that Britain adopted it or that other signatories would have accepted this interpretation.

evidence.note: The transcript quotes the six-inch deck-stiffening exception, proposes a twin mounting comparable in weight to a triple torpedo launcher, and criticizes the absence of torpedoes on British armed merchant cruisers.

segments.summary: A proposed twin six-inch mounting uses the treaty allowance for deck stiffening to explore how an armed merchant cruiser might later carry torpedoes.

segments.title: Foreign warship orders and a hypothetical British requisition
segments.body: Article 17 provides the starting point for a comparison with Britain's wartime acquisition of ships ordered by other countries. The account contrasts Turkish battleships in the First World War with destroyers in the Second World War, treating the latter as a repetition of the same British practice. A separate counterfactual asks what would have happened to an Argentine cruiser in British hands if war had begun in January 1939. With three triple turrets and a design compared to a modified Arethusa, the ship is imagined under a British name as the leader of an Arethusa squadron. The example distinguishes an actual requisition practice from a hypothetical fleet that depended on a different outbreak date.

evidence.note: Article 17 would prohibit wartime use of an undelivered foreign order, unlike Britain's earlier requisition of Turkish ships; in a January 1939 counterfactual, an Argentine cruiser with three triple turrets would lead an Arethusa squadron.

segments.summary: British use of ships ordered by foreign customers leads to a January 1939 counterfactual in which an Argentine cruiser joins an Arethusa squadron.

segments.title: Submarine bans and cruiser ratios that failed
segments.body: Even the 10,000-ton individual limit was open to manipulation: a cited British figure reached 10,400 tons, with some doubt attached to the official number. Britain's proposed submarine prohibition failed, as did an American attempt to extend capital-ship ratios to smaller vessels. A British alternative proposed 450,000 tons for the Royal Navy, 300,000 for the United States, and 250,000 for Japan. Some sketches justified Britain's allowance by allocating 150,000 tons for each major ocean in which it needed a force. Britain claimed commitments in the Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Pacific, with the Mediterranean adding another burden, while the United States faced two major oceans and Japan one. None of these proposals won agreement, leaving qualitative limits and allowing an effectively unlimited number of treaty-sized cruisers.

evidence.note: Negotiators rejected a British submarine ban and rival aggregate cruiser limits; Britain's proposal assigned tonnage according to Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Pacific commitments.

segments.summary: Negotiators rejected a British submarine ban and competing schemes for aggregate cruiser tonnage based on capital-ship ratios or worldwide commitments.

segments.title: Who shaped the treaty-cruiser ceiling?
segments.body: The familiar cruiser ceiling was not the inevitable outcome of the conference, and the precise origin of the proposal remains disputed in the account presented here. One version has American planners preparing to use the Omaha class as a baseline before Britain offered Hawkins, perhaps expecting another rejected proposal. Another interpretation is that Britain advanced the cap deliberately to prevent an unlimited cruiser race. A common 10,000-ton ceiling would not limit total numbers, but it could constrain the likely cost of each ship. Britain also expected other delegations to push its proposed tonnage ceiling somewhat higher.

evidence.note: Competing accounts identify either Britain's Hawkins or America's Omaha as the origin of the cruiser ceiling; Britain may have accepted it to cap each ship's cost.

segments.summary: Competing accounts identify Hawkins or Omaha as the model for the qualitative cruiser limit and offer different reasons for Britain's acceptance of the cap.

segments.title: Hawkins, Omaha, and Nagara as cruiser benchmarks
segments.body: Hawkins displaced about 12,500 tons at full load and carried seven 7.5-inch guns. Omaha mounted twelve six-inch weapons, eight in single mountings and four in two twin turrets, while Nagara carried seven 140 mm guns. Their quoted speeds were 31, 35, and 36 knots respectively. Omaha is described as having thicker armour in several respects than Hawkins, while Nagara had very little protection. Their torpedo batteries also differed. These lightly protected, transitional cruisers provided examples for the treaty's smaller-warship category before an international cruiser design standard had settled.

evidence.note: Hawkins displaced about 12,500 tons and carried seven 7.5-inch guns at 31 knots; Omaha carried twelve 6-inch guns at 35 knots with relatively heavier armour, while lightly protected Nagara carried seven 140 mm guns at 36 knots, and their torpedo batteries also differed.

segments.summary: A comparison of contemporary British, American, and Japanese cruisers shows the varied ships behind the treaty's new cruiser definition.

segments.title: Article 19 froze Pacific bases and defenses
segments.body: Article 19 assigned different restricted geography to the United States, British Empire, and Japan. For the United States, most Pacific insular possessions were frozen, the Aleutians remained within the restricted group, and Hawaii plus positions adjacent to the American mainland, Alaska, and the Panama Canal Zone were exempted. For Britain, Hong Kong and specified Pacific possessions east of 110 degrees east were frozen, with exceptions around Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. Japan's restricted possessions included the Kuril and Bonin islands, Formosa, and the Pescadores. Within the specified territories, the treaty barred new bases, greater repair capacity, and stronger coastal defences while permitting routine replacement of worn equipment. The strategic burden depended on where each power's homeland, industry, bases, and exempt positions lay.

evidence.note: Article 19 froze the status of bases and defences in specified American, British, and Japanese Pacific territories, barring new bases, expanded repair capacity, and stronger coastal defences while exempting defined American and British positions and allowing routine replacement.

segments.summary: Article 19 preserved the status quo across specified Pacific possessions by barring new bases, expanded repair capacity, and stronger coastal defenses.

segments.title: Why allowing Japanese fortification could aid containment
segments.body: Japan received neither its preferred fleet ratio nor freedom to strengthen many of its Pacific possessions. In this reading, that combination was strategically self-defeating: fixed defenses would have consumed Japanese resources without creating the offensive reach of ships or aircraft. Money sunk into coastal guns and island bases could not also fund the fleet or army, and an opponent could bypass many positions. Allowing stronger islands might therefore have supported a less humiliating compromise while still constraining Japan's ability to maneuver.

evidence.note: Fortifications as sunk costs that could reassure Japan while limiting spending on mobile forces.

segments.summary: Allowing island fortification could have reassured Japan while diverting money from mobile fleets and armies into positions opponents could bypass.

segments.title: How tactical bargaining success can undermine strategy
segments.body: The discussion asks whether the negotiators were thinking as naval strategists or simply pressing every advantage available at the conference. Tactical and professional competence differ from the ability to connect peacetime policy with the conditions of a future war. Restricting both Japan's fleet and its island defenses resembles terms imposed on a defeated enemy. Because Japan had fought with the victorious coalition, that apparent triumph in bargaining risked creating a more hostile strategic environment.

evidence.note: Tactical and professional skill did not guarantee a durable strategy, and restrictions resembling terms for a defeated power risked making Allied Japan more hostile.

segments.summary: The fortification settlement illustrates the difference between tactical bargaining success and a strategy designed to shape a safer postwar order.

segments.title: Why the equitable rewrite keeps the cruiser ceiling
segments.body: The equitable rewrite retains the Washington limits for ships below the capital-ship and carrier categories because an actual design precedent already exists. The same appeal to existing designs supports larger capital-ship allowances elsewhere in the proposed rewrite, so consistency rules out raising the cruiser ceiling merely to reach a larger or rounder figure. The Hawkins class and its 7.5-inch battery supply the historical benchmark. Had Churchill backed the proposed 9.2-inch alternative of roughly 15,000 to 18,000 tons, the precedent and therefore the treaty category could have been different.

evidence.note: The rewrite keeps the 10,000-ton cruiser ceiling because the ships actually built supported it; a 9.2-inch Hawkins of roughly 15,000 to 18,000 tons would have set another precedent.
The transcript explicitly connects retention of the cruiser ceiling to the use of actual design precedents when revising capital-ship tonnage.

segments.summary: The equitable rewrite keeps the 10,000-ton cruiser limit because an actual shipbuilding precedent supports it, while a larger Hawkins design could have changed the treaty category.

segments.title: How Hawkins shaped two decades of cruiser design
segments.body: The Hawkins class resembled an enlarged C- or D-class light cruiser and carried a scattered battery of seven 7.5-inch guns. One alternative considered here is five twin six-inch turrets using mountings like those fitted to Enterprise, which would still have required a larger hull. That arrangement, or the larger 9.2-inch design, could have changed both the ships and the later treaty boundary. The reason for choosing the 7.5-inch gun remains uncertain in this assessment, although availability is suggested as part of the explanation. Its inability to deal with the largest surface threats left torpedoes to provide a heavier striking weapon. This wartime emergency design nevertheless became a benchmark for cruiser construction for roughly twenty years, extending through the Second World War, despite its questionable combat efficiency.

evidence.note: The transcript evaluates Hawkins's layout, alternative armaments, torpedo role, and influence on treaty definitions.

segments.summary: A wartime emergency cruiser with awkward 7.5-inch armament became the benchmark for treaty cruisers through the Second World War.

segments.title: Geography made the Pacific freeze unequal
segments.body: For the United States, the Pacific was a broad defensive moat backed by a continental economy. Its homeland industry and exempt positions gave it reinforcement options that the treaty freeze did not erase. Britain operated at much greater distance but retained the ability to improve Singapore and other blocking positions. Japan, by contrast, was limited both in fleet tonnage and in its ability to build defense in depth across nearby islands, making formally shared restrictions strategically asymmetric.

evidence.note: Continental industry and exempt reinforcement positions favored the United States, Britain could strengthen Singapore, and Japan could not build comparable defensive depth under Article 19.

segments.summary: The same status-quo rule burdened Japan more heavily because the United States had a continental industrial base and Britain could strengthen Singapore outside the restricted area.

segments.title: Omaha joined old and new cruiser design ideas
segments.body: The Omaha class combined several generations of cruiser design. Twin turrets coexisted with casemate weapons mounted in conspicuous hull bulges. The design mixed pre-dreadnought cruiser practice, dreadnought-era ideas, and First World War technology. These wartime technologies would help shape later cruisers, especially those of the 1930s.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Omaha's turret and casemate arrangement to illustrate a hybrid of older cruiser ideas and wartime technology.

segments.summary: Omaha's turrets, casemates, and unusual hull gun positions show how postwar cruisers mixed pre-dreadnought practice with First World War lessons.

segments.title: A more equitable fortification compromise
segments.body: The proposed revision retains the ban on entirely new overseas fortifications but allows existing repair and maintenance facilities to modernize within their current footprint and with full disclosure to the other signatories. A limit on total area could be stretched by building upwards or downwards, so it would not prevent every increase in capacity. Coastal defences could be improved to the equivalent of cruiser armament, with a maximum gun calibre of eight inches and no proposed limit on the number of those guns. A base could therefore deter cruiser raids and resist initial operations while remaining vulnerable to a committed battle fleet. Japan could gain reassurance from being able to strengthen its islands, even though those positions would offer limited protection against capital ships.

evidence.note: The proposed compromise would let existing bases modernize within their disclosed footprints and allow coastal defenses up to eight inches, while continuing to bar new overseas fortifications.

segments.summary: The proposed rewrite allows existing bases to modernize within their footprint and permits coastal defenses up to eight-inch cruiser caliber.

segments.title: A durable treaty cannot leave one side feeling defeated
segments.body: In May 2022, debate over a future treaty ending the Russia-Ukraine war supplied a contemporary comparison for the Washington settlement. An agreement is unlikely to endure if one side celebrates outright victory while the other sees defeat. The final assessment returns to the failed proposals each Washington delegation rejected and asks whether the resulting bargain could be called equitable. Japan lost its preferred fleet ratio, freedom to fortify, and its British alliance, so many Japanese observers experienced the agreement as a defeat rather than an irritating compromise. American leaders also feared Japanese expansion and surrendered valuable ships to secure the deal. Treating the conference as a zero-sum contest deepened mutual insecurity instead of creating a stable deterrent order.

evidence.note: The transcript frames its May 2022 Russia-Ukraine reference as a treaty-design warning, then summarizes rejected proposals, Japanese perceptions of defeat, the alliance collapse, and mutual fear.

segments.summary: The conclusion links fleet limits, the fortification freeze, and the end of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance to a cycle of American and Japanese fear.

segments.title: Natori's dispersed seven-gun layout
segments.body: Natori is identified as a Nagara-class light cruiser. Her seven single guns were distributed around the hull, with three aft, two forward, and two wing mounts alongside the superstructure. This description provides a concrete example of the Japanese main-battery layout used in the comparison with Hawkins and Omaha.

evidence.note: Natori was a Nagara-class cruiser with three guns aft, two forward, and two wing mounts beside a superstructure. The surviving description does not establish whether that superstructure was forward or aft.

segments.summary: Natori's seven single guns were spread around the hull, providing a clear view of the Nagara class's main-battery arrangement.

segments.title: Japanese light cruisers emphasized torpedo attack
segments.body: Japanese light cruisers resembled large destroyers in their emphasis on torpedo attack. Nagara carried eight 24-inch tubes in four twin launchers, compared with six 21-inch tubes in the British and American examples discussed earlier. The larger weapons and more numerous launchers accompanied an increasing reliance on torpedoes as a major surface-ship weapon. This emphasis helps explain the importance of torpedo attack when considering later Imperial Japanese Navy surface doctrine and treaty debates.

evidence.note: Nagara's eight 24-inch torpedo tubes exceeded the six 21-inch tubes on the British and American cruisers, reflecting Japan's growing emphasis on torpedo attack.

segments.summary: Nagara and related Japanese light cruisers had a destroyer-like emphasis on torpedoes, with larger weapons and more tubes than the British and American examples discussed.
